The Torah Scholarship, State-Level Halakhic Rulings, and Public Activity of the Gaon Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli

This survey presents the life and teachings of Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli, defined as the halakhic architect of Jewish sovereignty in the modern era. The text traces his fascinating life trajectory, from his clandestine studies in the Soviet Union to his leadership of Yeshivat Merkaz HaRav and service on the Chief Rabbinical Court, while emphasizing his pioneering rulings that integrate Torah and state. The heart of the survey addresses his revolutionary innovations, such as defining the State of Israel as **"Malkhut Yisrael"** (Kingdom of Israel) possessing halakhic validity, solving complex agricultural issues through "Otzar Beit Din" (court treasury), and formulating an ethical doctrine for warfare and security. The article's purpose is to illuminate the Rabbi's persona as a living bridge between classical Lithuanian scholarship and the practical needs of a sovereign people in its land.

The Torah Scholarship, State-Level Halakhic Rulings, and Public Activity of the Gaon Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli

The Gaon Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli (5669–5755 / 1909–1995) stands as one of the pillars of halakhic jurisprudence and religious-Zionist thought in the twentieth century.[1, 2, 3] His multifaceted persona bridged geographical, historical, and ideological divides: from the Lithuanian Torah world immersed in clandestine study under the yoke of Communism, through pioneering spiritual leadership in an agricultural village, to the pinnacle of state-level halakhic ruling as a judge (dayyan) on the Chief Rabbinical Court and as head of Yeshivat Merkaz HaRav.[1, 3, 4] His Torah teaching was not limited to solving discrete problems, but rather established a complete theoretical-halakhic foundation, a kind of sovereign "meta-halakha," enabling the Torah of Israel to serve as a practical and political guide for the Jewish people returning to its land.[3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Childhood, Youth, and the "Miracle of Immigration": From the Lithuanian Torah World to Yeshivat Merkaz HaRav

Shaul Yisraeli was born on the 25th of Tammuz 5669 (July 14, 1909) in the city of Slutsk, Belarus, to Rabbi Benjamin Izraelit, who served as rabbi and head of the rabbinical court (av beit din) of the town of Koidanov in the Minsk province, and to Rabbanit Hava.[1, 4] His childhood and youth were shaped in the shadow of the rigid and oppressive Communist regime.[4] His father, who insisted on continuing to teach Torah despite severe governmental prohibitions, was captured and sent by the Soviets to Siberia, where his traces were lost, while his mother was later murdered by the Nazis.[4]

Despite the harsh conditions, he studied at a Talmud Torah and small yeshiva in Slutsk under the leadership of Lithuanian Torah luminaries, the Gaon Rabbi Yechezkel Abramsky and the yeshiva head Gaon Rabbi Isser Zalman Meltzer.[4] When the yeshiva in Slutsk was closed by the Yevsektsiya, he moved to Minsk and studied clandestinely with Rabbi Yehoshua Tsimblist of Horodna.[4] During this period, a governmental decree was issued in Minsk permitting only "professionals" to remain in the city; in order to survive and continue his studies, Rabbi Yisraeli learned the craft of cobblery, while his head and thoughts remained immersed in the world of the Gemara ("the dialectics of Abaye and Rava").[4] Subsequently, he joined a group of young men studying clandestinely in the "Maskil Le-Eitan" synagogue with Rabbi Avraham Eliyahu Meizel (who later became one of the leaders of Neturei Karta in Jerusalem).[4] Rabbi Yisraeli attributed decisive importance to this period, noting that Rabbi Meizel was the one who "set him on his feet" from a scholarly and methodological standpoint.[4]

In the year 5690 (1930), in light of the tightening Soviet stranglehold, he moved to Moscow in an attempt to emigrate legally.[4] When these attempts failed, he began planning a clandestine and illegal escape together with his study companion from Minsk, Rabbi David Solomon (later rabbi of Kfar Avraham), and Rabbi Avraham Shadmi (later head of Kollel Beit Zevul and son-in-law of Rabbi Y. M. Charlap).[4] Because of the mortal danger involved in crossing the border, the three turned to the Gaon Rabbi Yaakov Klemes in Moscow to decide for them by conducting the "Goral HaGra" (lot of the Vilna Gaon).[4] The lot fell on an explicit biblical verse from Deuteronomy:

"Turn and take your journey, and come to the Amorite mountain and to all its neighboring places, in the Arabah, in the hill country and in the lowland and in the Negev and by the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and the Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates" (Deuteronomy 1:7) [4]

Following this dramatic resolution of doubt, the three set out and on the 23rd of Shevat 5693 (1933), in the dead of night while wrapped in white sheets for camouflage against the snow, they crossed the frozen Prut River at the Polish border.[4] They were captured by the Polish border guard and taken into custody with the threat of deportation back to the Soviet Union—a certain death sentence.[4] At the height of the crisis, they sent a letter to Maran Rabbi Avraham Yitzchak HaCohen Kook in Jerusalem.[4] Rav Kook acted immediately, personally appealed to the British High Commissioner, and obtained certificates (entry permits) for them.[4] Until their actual immigration, Rabbi Yisraeli studied at the distinguished Mir Yeshiva in Poland.[4]

At the beginning of 5694 (1934) he immigrated to the Land and began his studies at Yeshivat Merkaz HaRav.[4] Rav Kook immediately recognized his phenomenal genius and chose him to be one of three select students (together with Rabbi Yehuda Gershuni and Rabbi David Hanzen) before whom he would lecture and prepare his general lesson before delivering it to the yeshiva.[4] Simultaneously, a deep spiritual and scholarly bond was forged between him and the Gaon Rabbi Yaakov Moshe Charlap, with whom he studied in a regular ḥavruta (study partnership).[4] In the year 5698 (1938) Rabbi Yisraeli received rabbinic ordination (semikhah) from Rabbi Charlap, and in that same year he traveled to Poland and married his cousin, Bat-Sheva née Burgensky.[4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Period of Kfar HaRoeh: Pioneering Halakha and Charting the Path of Torah on the Land's Soil

Upon his ordination, Rabbi Yisraeli was appointed to serve as rabbi of the pioneering agricultural moshav Kfar HaRoeh (named after Rav Kook).[4] Rabbi Yisraeli established his residence in the village and served there for approximately 28 years.[4] During this period he developed an unprecedented model of communal Torah life interwoven with productive agricultural work.[4]

Modern agriculture in the Land of Israel posed pioneering and complex halakhic questions for which no explicit answer was found in the traditional rabbinic literature of the Diaspora.[3] Rabbi Yisraeli labored to solve these problems from the primary sources, while incorporating practical scientific understanding and close consultation with agronomists and experts.[4] Among the central issues he resolved were:

Milking on Shabbat: Finding halakhic and technological solutions that prevent a Torah-level prohibition (issur de-oraita) of extracting, while preventing animal suffering and economic collapse of the religious dairy farm.[4]

Kilayim (prohibited mixtures) of seeds and grafting of trees: Addressing modern planting methods, such as the issue of planting vetch and oats together as fodder.[3, 4]

Laws of the Sabbatical year (shemitah): Formulating practical solutions for maintaining Jewish agriculture during shemitah without collapsing the new settlement.[3, 4]

He presented his lectures and historic rulings on these matters in his pioneering work "Eretz Ḥemdah" (Desirable Land).[1, 3, 4] The first part of the book was symbolically completed on the 5th of Iyar 5708 (the day of the State's declaration), as an expression of the recognition that the state's resurrection demands a sovereign halakhic-agricultural code.[3, 4] By virtue of these rulings, Rabbi Yisraeli was already recognized as the leading authority in the State of Israel on commandments dependent on the Land, and for many years he headed the Chief Rabbinate's designated committee on this subject.[3, 4]

Parallel to his agricultural activity, he served as rosh metivta (head of the advanced academy) and taught the advanced class at Yeshivat Kfar HaRoeh, founded in 1940.[4] At that time, Rabbi Yehoshua Yagel, head of Midrashiyat Noam, approached him with a request to establish the subject of "Maḥshevet Yisrael" (Jewish Thought) as a worthy intellectual alternative for religious youth against the winds of socialism, Marxism, and national secularism of those days.[3, 4] Rabbi Yisraeli accepted the challenge, defined the curriculum, worked to have the subject recognized by the Ministry as a mandatory matriculation subject, and composed for it the leading anthology "Perakim be-Maḥshevet Yisrael" (Chapters in Jewish Thought).
which serves to this day as a foundational educational work.[1, 3, 4]

A unique and less well-known chapter from this period was Rabbi Isra'eli's intention to establish a practical agricultural yeshiva, stemming from a vision to create an organic synthesis between the highest level of theoretical study and working the land and settlement of the border.[5]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Return to Jerusalem: Rabbinical Judge, Yeshiva Headship and Statehood Leadership

At the beginning of the winter semester of 5719 (1959), in light of significant growth in the number of students at Yeshivat Merkaz HaRav and the passing of the Rosh Yeshiva Rabbi Ya'akov Kalav, the yeshiva students approached the Rosh Yeshiva, Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook, with a request to strengthen the teaching staff.[4] Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda sent the students to Kfar HaRo'eh to urge Rabbi Isra'eli to come and teach in the yeshiva.[4] Rabbi Isra'eli initially hesitated, out of humility and reverence, saying: "For years I have engaged in halakhah; a general shi'ur in a yeshiva is something else, that is scholarship...".[4] He ultimately acceded, and for thirty-six (36) years delivered the central general shi'ur in the yeshiva.[4]

His profound humility and the holy trembling he felt toward his teachers found expression in his first shi'ur in the yeshiva (in its old building in 'Beit HaRav').[4] When the students asked him to ascend to the platform by the Holy Ark, Rabbi Isra'eli went up three steps, kissed the curtain, and then descended one step, saying: "In the place where Rabbi Kook stood I cannot stand".[4]

In the year 5725 (1965) he was appointed to serve as a judge on the Supreme Rabbinical Court for Appeals in Jerusalem, and consequently moved to reside in the city.[4] On the Supreme Court he served alongside the Torah giants Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv and Rabbi Ovadiah Yosef, and earned their immense esteem.[3] The great ultra-Orthodox Torah scholars viewed him as a posek of rare stature and even attempted to lead an initiative to appoint him as Chief Rabbi of Israel.[3, 5] Rabbi Isra'eli served as a judge until his retirement in the year 5740 (1980).[4] Concurrently, he served as a member of the editorial board of the scholarly-Torah commentary on the Bible "Da'at Mikra".[4]

After the passing of Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda Kook in the year 5742 (1982), Rabbi Isra'eli was appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Merkaz HaRav alongside the Gaon Rabbi Avraham Elkana Kahana Shapira.[4] During this period he became famous for his statist lectures and sermons at the Yom Yerushalayim assemblies, which expressed a robust and uncompromising Religious Zionist worldview.[4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Statist Doctrine: Defining the State as "Malkhut Yisra'el"

Rabbi Isra'eli's public activity gained special momentum with the establishment of the State in the year 5708 (1948).[4] Together with a group of prominent rabbis, he founded the "Council of Rabbis of HaPo'el HaMizrachi," which was intended to provide authoritative halakhic responses to the practical questions of the new state.[1, 4] He served as the spokesman of the organization and edited its famous journal "HaTorah veHaMedinah," which became the central platform for clarifying matters of public halakhah, internal security, coalition politics and taxation.[1, 3] In addition, he was the one who formulated the prayer text for Independence Day and instituted the convening of 'Yarchei Kallah' gatherings.[4]

At the heart of his statist doctrine stood a revolutionary halakhic definition of the modern State of Israel [3]:

The Transition from Private Community to an All-Israel Framework

Rabbi Isra'eli emphasized that the establishment of the State marked the emergence of the people of Israel from dogmatic communal frameworks in the Diaspora to a sovereign all-Israel framework.[3] Consequently, the commandments of settling the Land and applying sovereignty over it are not merely private individual commandments, but public commandments belonging to the national public domain.[3]

The Status of Democratic Government

In his foundational essay from 5708, Rabbi Isra'eli determined that the State of Israel is defined halakhically as "Malkhut Yisra'el" in every respect.[3] According to his approach, there is no need for an anointed king in order to apply the laws of kingship, since an elected democratic government derives its state and halakhic authority from the consent of "Klal Yisra'el."[3] This essay continues to guide to this day the poskim and scholars who discuss the halakhic authority of the government in Israel.[3]

Multi-disciplinary Halakhic Rulings

Rabbi Isra'eli was endowed with comprehensive ability to issue rulings in all areas of Torah.[3] In an essay by Rabbi Ya'akov Ariel, Rabbi Isra'eli was compared to a "village doctor" – one who is required to have absolute and simultaneous mastery of general medicine, surgery, diagnosis and treatment, without the privilege of narrow specialization.[3] Thus Rabbi Isra'eli mastered talmudic analysis, monetary laws, the laws of Shabbat and prohibited and permitted matters, alongside the commandments dependent on the Land and the laws of army and state.[3]

A prominent symbol of his statist multi-disciplinary rulings was his leading of the principled ruling (joined by Chief Rabbis Avraham Shapira and Mordechai Eliyahu) accepting the definition of brain-respiratory death as complete death according to halakhah.[3] This bold medical ruling enabled the harvesting of organs for transplantation to save critically ill patients, and constituted a dramatic bridge between classical halakhah and modern medical science.[3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Laws of Shemittah: Otzar Beit Din as the "King's Highway" Le-Khatehillah

One of the subjects in which Rabbi Isra'eli's agricultural-statist doctrine found its most distinctive expression was the approach to shemittah, and particularly the historical dispute between the mechanism of "heter mekhirah" and the institution of "otzar beit din."[6, 7]

While heter mekhirah is based on a legal stratagem that temporarily removes Jewish ownership of the land in order to circumvent the prohibitions of shemittah (something that drew sharp halakhic criticism from poskim such as the Netziv and the Hazon Ish due to the prohibition of "lo teḥonnem" and the sale of land in Eretz Yisra'el) [6], Rabbi Isra'eli viewed the institution of otzar beit din as the proper solution and preferred it le-khatehillah.[7]

Rabbi Isra'eli based his ruling on several theoretical and practical principles:

Defining the Essence of Shemittah

The fundamental principle of the shemittah year is the negation of private ownership and the application of the concept of hefker to the land.[7] This principle is fulfilled completely and in the finest manner when the farmer transfers management of his fields to the beit din acting as agent of the public.[7] The beit din does not trade in produce (something forbidden during shemittah), but rather collects from consumers only the costs and handling fees.[7] Therefore, Rabbi Isra'eli determined that "otzar beit din is the sole response to fulfilling the commandment in practice... it is not a last-resort solution, but the king's highway le-khatehillah."[7]

Exemption from Bi'ur

Based on the approach of the Ramban, Rabbi Isra'eli ruled that produce gathered in otzar beit din does not require the obligation of bi'ur (which applies to private produce when it is finished for the beast from the field), since this produce is already defined as removed from the house and is in the public domain.[7]

Thanks to his intensive activity and halakhic elucidation, a significant change occurred in religious agricultural settlement [7]:

In previous shemittot, religious kibbutzim tended to sign onto "heter mekhirah" out of fear of economic losses, but under his guidance 10 leading religious kibbutzim joined the framework of "otzar beit din."[7]

This trend created great sanctification of God's name and led to lowering the prices of fruits and vegetables in the shemittah year, contrary to the claims of private marketers.[7]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Qibya Affair and War Ethics in Halakhah

The Qibya incident in 1953 (Operation Shoshana), carried out as a response to the murder of a Jewish family in Kfar Yehud by Arab infiltrators, sparked widespread international and public controversy due to harm to the civilian population and to children.[8] Rabbi Isra'eli published in the journal "HaTorah veHaMedinah" a monumental halakhic study entitled "The Qibya Incident in Light of Halakhah," which constitutes to this day the most fundamental and comprehensive work on the law of war and Jewish combat ethics in the modern era.[3, 8]

Rabbi Isra'eli conducted a gradual and incisive analysis of the issue of harming innocent civilians while making a sharp distinction between criminal and personal law and
Military and Governmental Law [8]:

A. Responsibility of a Population that Encourages and Assists Terror

Rabbi Yisraeli investigated whether collective criminal responsibility can be imposed upon a village population that supports terrorists.[8] He discussed a midrash in Bereshit Rabbah (34:19) which establishes that under the Noahide laws there exists agency for transgression in murder (that is, one who hires or sends another to murder is liable to capital punishment by a court).[8] He interpreted the dispute between the author of "Mishpat HaMelukhah" (Rabbi Isser Zalman Meltzer) and the "Mishneh LaMelekh," who debated whether the liability derives from the law of actual "agency" or from the law of "indirect causation."[8]

Rabbi Yisraeli ruled in accordance with the opinion of Rambam, who disputed the midrash and held that there is no agency for transgression among Noahides.[8] Consequently, a civilian population that merely encourages terror in a passive manner cannot be sentenced to death.[8] He also discussed the dispute between Rambam and Ramban regarding the obligation of "laws" among Noahides (the case of Shimon and Levi in Shechem).[8] Rambam held that the people of Shechem were liable to death because they did not judge Shechem son of Hamor, whereas Ramban held that they were not killed for nullifying the obligation of laws but rather because they were wicked and idolaters.[8] Rabbi Yisraeli ruled halakhically that a civilian population may not be harmed merely because it refrained from eliminating terrorists from its midst, since this refraining may stem from duress and fear for their lives.[8]

However, when the population provides active assistance and refuge to assailants, they are subject to the law of "pursuer through indirect causation" (based on the reasoning of the "Or Sameah").[8] The entire adult population that provides physical and military assistance is considered halakhically as pursuers, and it is permitted to harm them in order to save the public, but this definition is in no way applicable to children.[8]

B. Harm to the Innocent in Private Law versus State Law

Rabbi Yisraeli discussed the Talmudic passage in tractate Bava Kamma dealing with King David's question whether it is permitted to save oneself with one's fellow's property.[8] According to Rashi this is forbidden, and according to Tosafot and the Rosh this is permitted (and it is ruled in Shulhan Arukh, section 359, that it is permitted to save oneself but one is obligated to pay for the damage).[8] In principle, a person is not permitted to save his life by killing his fellow ("What makes you think your blood is redder").[8] Therefore, in a private action, it is permitted to harm terrorists (according to the law of pursuer), but there is no halakhic permit whatsoever to harm innocent children who are in their proximity, since harming these children constitutes direct murder of those under duress.[8]

The approach changes completely when the action is defined as an official military action of the state [8]:

Legality of War ("Dina DeMalkhuta")

The permit to initiate war (which by its very nature entails bloodshed and harm to civilians) derives from international legal agreement between nation and nation, halakhically defined as "dina demalkhuta."[8]

Obligatory War and War of Vengeance

Rabbi Yisraeli determined categorically that war against assailants and terrorists who are engaged in continuous attack against us (even if they take breaks for their convenience) is defined as "obligatory war" according to all opinions.[8] War against enemies of Israel who retreat in order to return and attack is defined as a "war of vengeance," which is a commandment and to which full laws of war apply.[8]

Law of the Innocent in War

In war there is no obligation to be fastidious about operational details that would endanger the combatants in order to prevent indirect harm to enemy civilians, since such is the nature of war that "the righteous perish with the wicked."[8] The moral responsibility for the lives of the civilians and children who are harmed indirectly rests entirely upon the assailants who use them as human shields.[8]

Severe Limit to Combat Ethics

Rabbi Yisraeli emphasized in an unequivocal manner that even in the context of war, there is a severe prohibition against harming children and infants directly and with initial intent, and therefore there is a moral and operational obligation to endeavor and guard against this to the extent possible.[8]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Students, Institutions, and Recognition

Alongside his numerous books, Rabbi Yisraeli's legacy lives and pulsates through his distinguished students who serve as heads of yeshivot, judges, and city rabbis, and continue to lead the world of halakhah and state law.[1, 3]

His Prominent Students

Rabbi Yaakov Ariel: former Chief Rabbi of Ramat Gan and among the senior halakhic decisors of Religious Zionism.[1]

Rabbi Dov Lior: former Chief Rabbi of Kiryat Arba-Hebron and among the leading halakhic decisors.[1]

Rabbi Yosef Carmel: head of the "Eretz Hemdah" kollel and presiding judge of a rabbinical court.[1, 9]

Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi Amichai: head of the Torah VeHa'aretz Institute.[1]

Rabbi Moshe Harari: author of the popular halakhic series "Mikra'ei Kodesh."[1]

Rabbi Yehoshua Magnes: senior lecturer at Yeshivat Merkaz HaRav.[1]

The "Eretz Hemdah" Institute

In the year 5747 (1987), Rabbi Yisraeli established the "Eretz Hemdah" kollel and institute for rabbinical court studies in Jerusalem, and served as its president and spiritual guide.[4, 9] The institute was established with the blessing of the head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Avraham Shapira, and with the aim of uniting the elite of Religious Zionism and cultivating them to become Torah scholars and judges who would lead the rabbinical courts in Israel.[9] In the institute's faculty, Rabbi Yisraeli placed Torah scholars of the first rank, including the Gaon Rabbi Zalman Nehemia Goldberg, Rabbi Nahum Eliezer Rabinovitch, Rabbi Mordechai Greenberg, Rabbi Menahem Burstein, and Rabbi Yisrael Rosen.[9] After his passing, Rabbi Zalman Nehemia Goldberg and Rabbi Nahum Rabinovitch served as presidents of the institute, and subsequently his student Rabbi Yaakov Ariel was appointed to head it, while Rabbi Yosef Carmel serves as head of the kollel.[9]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Public Recognition and Honors

For his extensive work and prolific Torah scholarship, Rabbi Yisraeli was awarded prestigious state prizes and honors.[1, 4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Summary and Conclusions

The Gaon Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli will be remembered in the halakhic history of the Jewish people as the legal architect of renewed Jewish sovereignty.[3] While the exile forced the halakhic world to contract into the four cubits of the individual and the local community, Rabbi Yisraeli led a profound conceptual and decisional transformation that restored to the Torah its state-national dimension.[3]

His threefold contribution—development of modern agricultural halakhah through "Otzar Beit Din" and the commandments dependent on the Land [3, 7], establishment of the status of the state and its authorities as "Malkhut Yisrael" from a legal perspective [3], and formulation of a consistent doctrine of combat ethics and national defense [8]—laid the foundations for creative and sovereign religious-national life in the Land of Israel. His written legacy, his institutions, and his many students constitute living testimony to the work of a spiritual giant who succeeded in connecting heaven and earth, profound Lithuanian scholarship and practical Zionist pioneering.[1, 3, 4, 5]
